nameStory: The brush-tipped emerald gets its name from the unique shape of the male's claspers (the structures at the tip of his abdomen used for mating), which spread out like the bristles of a paint brush. This distinctive feature makes it one of the easier emerald dragonflies to identify when you can get a close look at a male.
description: The brush-tipped emerald is a medium-sized dragonfly with the characteristic metallic green sheen that gives all emerald dragonflies their name. Like other members of its family, it has a sturdy build with broad wings and typically measures about 2-2.5 inches long. The body appears dark bronze or blackish-green with a metallic luster that can shimmer in bright sunlight, and the wings are clear with dark veining.

idTips.label: Male claspers
idTips.description: Males have distinctive brush-like claspers at the tip of the abdomen that flare out like bristles - the key identifying feature that gives this species its name

idTips.label: Metallic body sheen
idTips.description: Body has a dark metallic green-bronze luster that catches the light with an almost oily rainbow sheen when viewed at different angles

idTips.label: Wing clarity
idTips.description: Wings are completely clear and glassy with no colored patches or bands, feeling thin and papery to the touch if handled

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with strong, direct wingbeats in a purposeful manner, often patrolling back and forth over water or woodland edges

idTips.label: Eye color
idTips.description: Large compound eyes appear bright green or blue-green and feel smooth and dome-like, meeting at the top of the head

habitat: Brush-tipped emeralds prefer wooded areas near clean streams, small rivers, and forest ponds throughout New England's mixed and deciduous forests. They're often found patrolling along shaded woodland edges and clearings where sunlight filters through the canopy. Look for them around acidic waters in areas with good forest cover, from lowland woods up to mid-elevation mountain slopes.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, usually not appearing until late May or early June when water temperatures warm sufficiently for development.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs from mid-June through August when adults are actively hunting, mating, and laying eggs. This is the best time to observe their distinctive flight patterns and identifying features.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall with some individuals still active through September, though numbers decline significantly as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off with the first hard frosts, while larvae overwinter in the muddy bottoms of streams and ponds, developing slowly through the cold months.

funFact: Despite being called 'emerald' dragonflies, these insects can actually see many more colors than humans can, including ultraviolet light - meaning the world looks completely different to them than it does to us, with patterns and colors on flowers, water, and even other dragonflies that are totally invisible to our eyes.
confusionNotes: The brush-tipped emerald is easily confused with other emerald dragonflies in the same genus, all of which have similar metallic green bodies and clear wings. The key is getting a good look at the male's distinctive brush-like claspers - if you see those flared bristles at the tail tip, you've found your brush-tipped emerald.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name Somatochlora literally means 'green body' in Greek, which describes the metallic sheen shared by all emerald dragonflies. However, this green coloration can appear quite different depending on lighting conditions and viewing angle, sometimes looking more bronze, copper, or even blackish.
compareHints: Among New England's many Somatochlora species, the brush-tipped emerald is most reliably distinguished by the male's unique claspers that flare outward like brush bristles. Other emeralds like the clamp-tipped or ski-tipped have differently shaped claspers (clamped together or ski-like respectively), while species like the mocha emerald have different body coloration patterns that can help separate them.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the many Somatochlora emeralds in New England, the Clamp-tipped stands out for its distinctive male appendages that look like mechanical clamps rather than the brush-like, curved, or pointed appendages of its relatives.
Among its emerald dragonfly relatives, the ski-tipped emerald is distinguished primarily by those characteristic curved male appendages that give it its name.
Among its Somatochlora relatives, the Mocha Emerald is unique for its brownish coloration - most other species in this genus display bright metallic greens and blues.
